t: Maximum Sum With at Most K Elements
o: Pick at most k cells from the grid, taking at most limits[i] cells from row i, maximizing the total. Because all values are non-negative and the only coupling between rows is the per-row cap, greedy exchange argument applies: sorting each row descending and truncating to its limit loses nothing, then taking the globally largest k remaining values is optimal. Example 2: rows truncated to [7] and [8,6], top 3 sum to 21.
k: Truncate each row to its limits[i] largest values first — extra values can never help.
All values are non-negative, so taking fewer than k is never forced to hurt; just take the top min(k, available) globally.
Total cells <= 250000, so a global sort is fast enough.

a.n: Approach 1: Truncate rows and global sort
a.i: Sort each row descending, cut at limits[i], pool everything, sort the pool descending, sum the first k entries.
s: Sort each row descending and keep the first limits[i] values.
a.t: O(N log N) where N = total cells, dominated by sorts

a.i: Instead of sorting the whole pool, stream the truncated values into a min-heap capped at size k; the heap ends holding the k largest values.
s: Build truncated per-row lists as in Approach 1.
Push each value; if heap size exceeds k, pop the minimum.
a.t: O(N log k) — heap operations dominate

w: Approach 1 is simplest and passes easily; mention the heap variant if asked for memory-conscious streaming. Watch for limits[i] = 0 rows and k = 0 (answer 0). Follow-up: if values could be negative, 'at most k' would require deciding whether to include each negative — the heap version handles it by only summing positives.
